title: The Devout Difference: Religion, Marital Quality, and Sex Among Americans | Institute for Family Studies
gist: IFS's FOCUS-sponsored 'Devout Difference' report: frequent churchgoing fell 49%->32% (1972-2024) and Catholic weddings fell 74% since 1970, yet churchgoers marry more, divorce less, report happier marriages and more/better sex. Value alignment (6.9x odds) and belief in marital permanence are the strongest predictors; Catholics show a puzzling stability gap, and orthodox FOCUS alumni outperform on stability.

themes.theme: Secular retreat from faith and marriage

insights.claim: Frequent US churchgoing (several times a month or more) fell from 49% to 32% between 1972 and 2024 per the General Social Survey, while the marriage rate fell more than 60% over the same period.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Long-run institutional decline underpinning falling household formation.
insights.quote: frequent churchgoing—several times a month or more—falling from 49% to 32% from 1972 to 2024

insights.claim: Weekly Mass attendance among self-identified Catholics fell from 44% in the 1970s to 18% today; Catholic weddings fell from 415,000 in 1970 to a COVID low of 97,000 and 109,000 in 2024.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Wedding-industry and Catholic institutional demand in secular decline.
insights.quote: The number of Catholic weddings stood at 415,000 in 1970 before falling to a historic low during COVID of 97,000

insights.claim: The share of married parents ages 20-54 attending religious services fell from 82% in the 1970s to 61%, and the share who are Catholic or Protestant fell from 91% to 61%; those rarely or never attending rose 57% between the 2010s and the post-COVID era.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Post-COVID acceleration of secularization among parents.
insights.quote: Between the 2010s and the post-COVID era, the share of married parents who rarely or never attend church increased by 57%.

insights.claim: The authors argue rising affluence and the welfare state eroded the practical necessity of marriage and religion, while 1960s-70s elites recast both as obstacles to self-actualization.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Frames family decline as partly a substitution effect of state/market provision.
insights.quote: Rising affluence and the growth of the welfare state further eroded both institutions’ practical necessity for financial and social survival.

insights.claim: The marriage gap between religious and secular Americans has widened since the 1970s: 60% of religious adults ages 20-54 are married today versus 42% of secular adults, up from a 10-point gap.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Religious-secular divergence in household formation is growing, not shrinking.
insights.quote: Today, 60% of religious Americans between ages 20 and 54 are married, compared to 42% of secular adults.

insights.claim: Net of age, education and race, churchgoing Americans ages 20-54 are 39% more likely to be married than non-churchgoers.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Religiosity remains a strong predictor of household formation after controls.

insights.claim: 54% of ever-married nominal Protestants ages 35-54 have divorced or separated, versus 34% of churchgoing Protestants, 27% of churchgoing Catholics, 36% of nominal Catholics and 40% of the non-religious.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Nominal affiliation without practice performs worst, even below secular Americans.
insights.quote: with 54% of ever-married nominal Protestants ages 35-54 having been divorced or separated

insights.claim: Studies suggest regular churchgoers are 30-50% less likely to divorce than non-religious Americans net of socioeconomic controls, though the Catholic figure likely reflects selection as divorced Catholics leave the faith.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Causal claim tempered by selection effects; useful caveat for interpreting religiosity data.

insights.claim: Being married is linked to a 151% increase in the odds of being very happy with life, but being happily married raises those odds by 545%.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Marital quality, not just status, is the big wellbeing lever.
insights.quote: Being married, for instance, is linked to a 151% increase in the odds of reporting being “very happy” with life—but being happily married increases those odds by 545 percent.

insights.claim: Churchgoers have 1.49 times higher odds of being happily married than non-religious spouses net of controls, while nominal Catholics and Protestants show no significant advantage over religious Nones, implying active participation rather than affiliation drives the effect.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Practice, not identity, is the active ingredient.
insights.quote: it is active church participation, not merely affiliation, that produces happier marriages

insights.claim: Only 48% of adults in a Pew poll consider shared moral and religious beliefs very important in choosing a partner, but the IFS survey finds value-aligned spouses have 6.85 times higher odds of being happy and 6.86 times higher odds of perceived stability.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Popular belief underweights the single strongest predictor of marital success; relevant to matchmaking/dating product design.
insights.quote: Most Americans do not believe that sharing similar moral and religious views matters much for forging a strong, stable marriage.

insights.claim: Among Protestants, 73% of value-aligned spouses are happily married versus just 18% of non-aligned; among Catholics the figures are 79% versus 38%.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Very large effect sizes for alignment.

insights.claim: Value alignment is the single strongest predictor of marital satisfaction for Christians: aligned spouses have a 78% predicted probability of a happy marriage versus 36% for non-aligned.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Ranks drivers: alignment > permanence belief > social support.
insights.quote: Value alignment is the single strongest predictor

insights.claim: Spouses who completely endorse marital permanence have 1.85 times higher odds of high marital satisfaction and 1.81 times higher odds of perceived stability; 52% of churchgoing Protestants and 39% of churchgoing Catholics hold this view versus 6% of Nones.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Commitment norms are a measurable, rare and potent asset.

insights.claim: Daily prayer is associated with 1.48 times higher odds of a stable marriage and 1.50 times higher odds of a happy one.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Ritual practice as a relationship-stability input.

insights.claim: Spouses who say their marriage is fair are 84% happily married versus 15% of those who disagree, and value-aligned spouses have 7.18 times higher odds of reporting a fair marriage.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Shared values reduce score-keeping; fairness mediates satisfaction.
insights.quote: 84% of these spouses are happily married, compared to just 15% of those who disagree with the same statement

insights.claim: Weekly sex among married Americans 20-54 fell from 64% in the 1990s to 54% today per the GSS; non-religious spouses fell from 61% to 48% while regular churchgoers are at 62%, creating a growing religious-secular divide.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Sex recession is concentrated among secular couples.
insights.quote: So, there is a growing religious-secular divide in married sex—and it favors religious couples.

insights.claim: In the IFS survey, 69% of churchgoing Catholics report weekly sex versus 47% of Nones; churchgoers have 1.49 times higher odds of weekly sex and 1.42 times higher odds of sexual satisfaction net of controls.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Overturns the trope of the frustrated religious believer.
insights.quote: The cultural trope of the sexually prudish, frustrated religious American does not fit the data.

insights.claim: Belief in marital permanence is a stronger predictor of sexual satisfaction than church attendance or prayer (1.53x odds of satisfaction, 1.31x odds of weekly sex).
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Commitment as 'aphrodisiac': security drives intimacy.
insights.quote: mutual commitment, by fostering greater investment, trust, and emotional security, functions as a powerful aphrodisiac

insights.claim: Catholics open to having children have 1.69 times higher odds of sexual satisfaction than those who are not.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Pronatalist orientation correlates with relationship satisfaction.

insights.claim: 84% of married FOCUS alumni endorse marriage as a permanent commitment, versus 39% of churchgoing Catholics, 52% of churchgoing Protestants and 6% of Nones.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Campus ministry formation produces markedly different norms.

insights.claim: Among couples married 10 years or less, 95% of FOCUS alumni perceive their marriage as stable versus 65% of churchgoing Catholics, giving 5.24 times higher odds net of controls; their happiness edge is modest and largely explained by age.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Stability, not happiness, is where orthodox formation shows up; sponsor-funded data warrants caution.

insights.claim: Net of controls, churchgoing Catholics have 2.68 times higher odds of sexual satisfaction than married FOCUS alumni, which the authors attribute to youth, short marriages (5.1 years) and likely natural family planning (91% open to life).
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Shows the report includes adverse findings for its sponsor.

insights.claim: Roughly 22% and 36% of first marriages end in separation or divorce by years five and 10 respectively.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Baseline early-marriage dissolution hazard.

insights.claim: Catholics report lower perceived marital stability than Protestants and Nones (63% of churchgoing Catholics vs 77% of churchgoing Protestants and 71% of Nones) despite higher satisfaction and lower divorce: they divorce less but worry more.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Puzzle suggests reactive rather than proactive church support.
insights.quote: Catholics appear to divorce less but worry about marital stability more

insights.claim: More church support predicts more stable Protestant marriages but less stable Catholic marriages, possibly because Catholic families turn to the church only after instability sets in.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Delivery model (proactive vs reactive) of community support matters.

insights.claim: Only 46% of churchgoing Catholic parents and 57% of churchgoing Protestant parents report even some help from their church community, and Catholic families with three or more children report lower marital satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Unmet demand for family support services among large, mobile religious families.
insights.quote: only 46% of churchgoing Catholic parents report receiving even “some help” from their church community

insights.claim: Religious believers facing mental health problems typically seek help from clergy rather than therapists, fueling growth in the Christian mental health field such as the Catholic Psychotherapy Association and CAPS.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Growth niche: value-aligned therapy services.
insights.quote: There has been a growing sensitivity to this need in recent years, and as such, the field of Christian mental health is growing.

insights.claim: GSS data show the religiously married ages 20-54 have avoided the recent US happiness crash better than any group, being more than twice as likely to be very happy as peers not tethered to faith and marriage.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Wellbeing bifurcation along family/faith lines; relevant to social stability and policy.
insights.quote: Men and women tethered to the institutions of faith and marriage are more than twice as likely to be very happy today

insights.claim: The authors recommend upstream investment in adolescent and young adult formation (parishes, schools, campus ministries) as the most promising lever for marital stability.
insights.speaker: Rich Dell’Isola, Brad Wilcox, Grant Bailey and Jane Lankes Smith
insights.so_what: Points to where pro-family philanthropy/policy may flow.
insights.quote: Investing early in this kind of formation is not a departure from strengthening marriage and family life
